Fix \(S\in\mathcal I\), put \(U=V\setminus S\) and \(O=X\setminus S\), and write \(A=Q^{-1}\), so \(C=A_{X,:}\).  Assumption \(\text{ass:regime-solvability}\) gives inverses of \(Q=Q_{V,V}\) and \(Q_{U,U}\), because \(\varnothing,S\in\mathcal I\).  With the determinant of a zero-dimensional matrix equal to one, block elimination in the order \((S,U)\) gives
\[
 \det Q=\det(Q_{U,U})
 \det\!\left(Q_{S,S}-Q_{S,U}Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}\right)
\]
and
\[
 A_{S,S}=\left(Q_{S,S}-Q_{S,U}Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}\right)^{-1}.
\]
Both factors in the determinant formula are nonzero; hence
\[
 \det(C_{S,S})=\det(A_{S,S})
 =\frac{\det(Q_{U,U})}{\det Q}\ne0.                                \tag{5}
\]

The \((U,S)\) block of \(QA=I_N\) gives
\[
 A_{U,S}=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,S}A_{S,S}.
\]
Since \(Q_{U,S}=-B_{U,S}\), restriction to the rows \(O\) and (5) yield
\[
 T_S(C)=C_{O,S}C_{S,S}^{-1}
 =\bigl[Q_{U,U}^{-1}B_{U,S}\bigr]_{O,:}.                             \tag{6}
\]
The \((U,U)\) block of \(QA=I_N\), together with the preceding identity, gives
\[
 A_{U,U}-Q_{U,U}^{-1}B_{U,S}A_{S,U}=Q_{U,U}^{-1}.
\]
Consequently \(R_S(C)\) has zero columns on \(S\) and equals \((Q_{U,U}^{-1})_{O,:}\) on \(U\).

By \(\text{ass:perfect-intervention}\), the nonintervened equations under \(\operatorname{do}(X_S=x)\) are
\[
 Q_{U,U}V_U=\varepsilon_U+B_{U,S}x.
\]
Equations (5)--(6) therefore prove on the structural probability space that
\[
 X_O^{\operatorname{do}(X_S=x)}=R_S(C)\varepsilon+T_S(C)x,
\]
and hence
\[
 K_S^{B,\varepsilon}(x)
 =\mathcal L\bigl(R_S(C)\varepsilon+T_S(C)x\bigr).                   \tag{7}
\]
Observationally, \(X=C\varepsilon\), so
\[
 R_S(C)\varepsilon=X_O-T_S(C)X_S.                                   \tag{8}
\]
Thus the observational law determines the residual law in (8), and that law together with \(T_S(C)\) determines (7) for every \(x\).

No expectation is required to identify the response matrix from the full kernel.  Write \(\mu_S=K_S(0)\).  Equation (7) says \(K_S(x)=\tau_{T_S(C)x}\mu_S\).  By \(\text{lem:probability-translation-rigidity}\), \(T_S(C)\) is the unique linear map having this property (with the unique empty map when \(O=\varnothing\)).  Hence the kernel itself identifies the response slope even for sources without first moments.  Finally, if \(C_{:,i}=0\), the defining formula for \(R_S(C)\) gives \(R_S(C)_{:,i}=0\) for every \(S\).  Therefore an observationally invisible source stays invisible under every allowed intervention.  The calculation includes \(S=\varnothing\), \(U=\varnothing\), \(O=\varnothing\), and zero residual columns under the stated empty-matrix conventions.

We prove directed containment.  Suppose first that
\(\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G)\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H)\), and fix \(C\in\mathcal D_G\).  By \(\text{thm:exact-mixing-realization}\), there is an exact-support matrix \(Q=I_N-B\) on \(G\), with all required principal systems invertible, whose observed mixing matrix is \(C\).  Equip its visible columns with the independent two-point diagnostic sources \(\xi^C\) from \(\text{lem:diagnostic-mixture-rigidity}\), and equip its zero columns with arbitrary independent nonconstant non-Gaussian sources.  The broadened exact-support model class imposes no location or moment restriction, so this is an admissible \(G\)-mechanism.

By the assumed containment, its complete kernel tuple is generated by one admissible \(H\)-mechanism; denote that mechanism's observed mixing matrix by \(D\) and its common source vector by \(\eta\).  Exact mixing realization gives \(D\in\mathcal D_H\).  Equality of the observational kernels is
\[
 \mathcal L(C\xi^C)=\mathcal L(D\eta).
\]
The diagnostic rigidity lemma therefore supplies a surjection \(f:U_C\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero \(a_i\) such that
\[
 C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\qquad(i\in U_C).                              \tag{9}
\]

Fix \(S\in\mathcal I\).  By the intervention-pushforward lemma, the two equal kernels have representations
\[
 K_S(x)=\tau_{T_S(C)x}\mu_{C,S}
       =\tau_{T_S(D)x}\mu_{D,S},
 \qquad
 \mu_{C,S}=\mathcal L(R_S(C)\xi^C),\quad
 \mu_{D,S}=\mathcal L(R_S(D)\eta).
\]
At \(x=0\), the two residual laws agree.  The translation-rigidity lemma then gives \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\), including the empty-output case.  Thus \((D,f,a)\) satisfies every clause of \(\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\).

Conversely, assume \(\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\) and take an arbitrary admissible \(G\)-mechanism with observed mixing matrix \(C\) and source vector \(\varepsilon\).  Exact mixing realization places \(C\) in \(\mathcal D_G\).  Select a cover witness \((D,f,a)\).  The same realization theorem constructs an admissible exact-support coefficient matrix on \(H\) with observed mixing matrix \(D\).  For every \(j\in U_D\), put
\[
 \eta_j=\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\varepsilon_i.                             \tag{10}
\]
The fibers are nonempty and disjoint, so these sources are mutually independent.  They are nonconstant by \(\text{lem:independent-sum-nondegenerate}\), and they are non-Gaussian by \(\text{lem:levy-cramer-decomposition}\): a Gaussian sum would force every nonconstant summand to be Gaussian.  Add arbitrary independent legal sources on the zero columns of \(D\).  This constructs one admissible target source tuple, with no appeal to means or variances.  Equation (9) gives \(C\varepsilon=D\eta\).

For every \(S\), equality of the response matrices and (9) imply, column by column,
\[
 R_S(C)_{:,i}
 =C_{X\setminus S,i}-T_S(C)C_{S,i}
 =a_iR_S(D)_{:,f(i)}\qquad(i\in U_C).                               \tag{11}
\]
If \(i\notin U_C\), then \(C_{:,i}=0\), and the intervention-pushforward lemma gives \(R_S(C)_{:,i}=0\).  Surjectivity of \(f\), (10), and (11) therefore give
\[
 R_S(C)\varepsilon=R_S(D)\eta.
\]
Together with \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\), equation (7) proves equality of the two kernels for every \(x\), using the same \(D\) and the same \(\eta\) in all regimes.  Hence
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G)\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H).
\]
Applying the directed statement in both orders proves the equality criterion.  Exact mixing realization retains every punctured-fiber and Hall--Rado boundary, while the diagnostic lemma retains zero columns, proportional columns, source symmetries, and lower-dimensional cancellations.  Thus no generic, closure, centering, or moment condition has entered the population equivalence theorem.

We expose the finite formula before invoking elimination.  For each local system in \(\mathcal D_G\), a rank equality is the finite disjunction over possible ranks that one selected minor is nonzero and all larger minors vanish.  On such a pivot chart, Gaussian elimination expresses an affine base point and a basis of the direction space of \(\mathcal A_j(C)\) as rational functions whose denominators are precisely the selected nonzero minors.  Adjoining the base point yields a rational spanning matrix for \(W_j(C)\).  For every \(J\subseteq L\), the Hall--Rado condition is the finite disjunction of minors expressing
\[
 \operatorname{rank}[W_j(C):j\in J]\ge |J|.
\]
Multiplication by chart denominators converts it to integral polynomial sign conditions without changing it on that chart.  The punctured-coordinate tests and the intervention determinants are likewise finite rank or nonvanishing conditions.  By \(\text{thm:exact-mixing-realization}\), the resulting quantifier-free formula \(\operatorname{Dom}_G(C)\) defines exactly \(\mathcal D_G\), including lower-dimensional chart intersections.

For visible sets \(U,W\subseteq V\) and a surjection \(f:U\twoheadrightarrow W\), introduce at most \(N\) nonzero scalar variables \(a_i\), and impose
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &C_{:,i}=0\Longleftrightarrow i\notin U,
 &&D_{:,j}=0\Longleftrightarrow j\notin W,\\
 &a_i\ne0,
 &&C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\quad(i\in U).
\end{aligned}                                                         \tag{12}
\]
Column nonzeroness is the strict polynomial inequality \(\sum_{r\in X}C_{ri}^2>0\).  On the domain charts, response equality is imposed without an inverse by
\[
 C_{X\setminus S,S}\operatorname{adj}(C_{S,S})\det(D_{S,S})
 =D_{X\setminus S,S}\operatorname{adj}(D_{S,S})\det(C_{S,S})          \tag{13}
\]
for every \(S\in\mathcal I\).  The domain conditions make both determinants nonzero, so (13) is equivalent to \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\).

Let \(\Theta_f(C,D,a)\) conjoin \(\operatorname{Dom}_H(D)\), (12), and all equations (13).  The directed compiler decides
\[
 \forall C\in\mathbb R^{n\times N}\left[
 \operatorname{Dom}_G(C)\Longrightarrow
 \bigvee_{U,W,f}\exists D\in\mathbb R^{n\times N}
 \exists a\in\mathbb R^U\ \Theta_f(C,D,a)\right].                  \tag{14}
\]
By the unrestricted source-partition theorem and the coupled-equivalence theorem, (14) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{Cover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\).  Structural coefficients were eliminated by the explicit affine and Hall--Rado realization theorem, and source laws by the explicit diagnostic/source-partition theorem, before real-algebraic elimination is applied.

We verify the advertised conservative counts.  A matrix with at most \(N\) rows and columns has at most \(2^{2N}\) minors.  Selecting pivot data for at most \(N\) local systems gives at most \(2^{2N^2}\) joint charts.  A concatenated Hall matrix has at most \(N\) rows and \(N^2\) columns and therefore fewer than \(2^{N+N^2}\) minors.  The \(2^\ell\) Hall subfamilies, the \(q\) intervention blocks, and all zero-pattern formulas contribute less than \((q+N+1)2^{4N^2}\) after sharing repeated atoms.  Finally, visible subsets and source maps number at most
\[
 2^{2N}(N+1)^N\le2^{3N^2}\qquad(N\ge2).
\]
Thus the number of distinct input polynomials is at most
\[
 s=(q+N+1)2^{8N^2}.
\]
Pivot minors have degree at most \(N\).  A cleared Hall minor contains at most \(N\) rational entries, and clearing at most \(N\) chart denominators gives degree below \(d=4N^3\); (12)--(13) have no larger degree.  Leibniz expansion across fewer than \(2^{8N^2}\) recorded atoms is bounded by the coefficient bit length
\[
 \tau=(\lambda+1)2^{8N^2}.
\]
These inequalities also cover empty blocks and zero minors.

Formula (14) has a universal block of size \(p=nN\) and an existential block of size at most \(p+N\).  Applying \(\text{lem:effective-real-quantifier-elimination}\) with these displayed \(s,d,\tau\) yields
\[
 \mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)
 =(  au+1)^2(s+1)^{(p+1)(p+N+1)+1}
 (d+1)^{c_{\mathrm{qe}}(p+1)(p+N+1)}
\]
bit operations after increasing its one absolute constant once.  Its sign conditions and algebraic sample descriptions certify the answer, and zero signs retain forced zeros, nullification, and boundary cells.  Running (14) in both directions costs at most \(2\mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)\).

There are exactly \(2^{N(N-1)}\) labeled loopless digraphs.  Test each against \(G\).  To quotient only by latent relabeling, choose the lexicographically least adjacency encoding among the \(\ell!\) simultaneous row-and-column permutations that fix all observed labels; each comparison costs at most \(N^2\) bit operations.  This gives
\[
 2^{N(N-1)}\bigl(2\mathsf B(N,q,\lambda)+\ell!\,N^2\bigr)
\]
bit operations, apart from fixed linear encoding overhead, and proves termination and completeness of the enumeration.

Fix \(S\).  The intervention-pushforward lemma writes every kernel as
\[
 K_S(x)=\tau_{T_S(C)x}\mathcal L(R_S(C)\varepsilon).
\]
For two equal kernels, evaluation at zero equates the residual laws, and \(\text{lem:probability-translation-rigidity}\) then equates their response matrices.  Applying \(\text{lem:finite-mixture-containment-unrestricted}\) to the residual matrices gives exactly the visible-column source surjection and proportionalities defining \(\mathcal W_S(C)\).  Conversely, those proportionalities permit the grouped-source construction in that lemma, and equality of the response matrices then reproduces the full affine kernel.  Quantifying over \(C\in\mathcal D_G\) proves the regime-wise assertion without moments.

Because \(\varnothing\in\mathcal I\), \(R_\varnothing(C)=C\) and \(T_\varnothing\) is the unique empty map.  A joint witness must therefore begin at a member \((D,f,a)\in\mathcal W_\star(C)\).  If this root also satisfies \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\) for every \(S\), then for each \(i\in U_C\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 R_S(C)_{:,i}
 &=C_{X\setminus S,i}-T_S(C)C_{S,i}\\
 &=a_i\bigl(D_{X\setminus S,f(i)}-T_S(D)D_{S,f(i)}\bigr)
 =a_iR_S(D)_{:,f(i)}.                                                  \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
Columns nullified by (18) are omitted from the residual visible set, and fibers may merge further; the finite-mixture theorem permits both.  Thus one observational root induces compatible witnesses at every regime vertex.  Conversely, one common target mechanism has one observed mixing matrix \(D\), and diagnostic observational equality supplies one root partition; translation rigidity applied to each complete response kernel supplies all simultaneous response equalities.  Hence a global section exists exactly when all regime vertices attach to one such root, and then every transition composition is automatically the identity on the induced common columns.

The sets involved are finite unions of the pivot, zero-pattern, surjection, proportionality, and response sign charts in the effective compiler.  A transition edge adds only polynomial equalities of common \(D\)-coordinates and the induced relations (18).  Therefore the rooted-section condition is a finite semialgebraic test decided by that compiler.  Applying the argument in both directions proves the final equality characterization.  Separate nonempty regime fibers need not choose one common root; the proposition states precisely the additional condition rather than assuming it.

Let \(k,r\in\mathbb N_0\), let \(\mu\) be a probability law on \(\mathbb R^k\), and write \(	au_h\mu\) for its translate by \(h\in\mathbb R^k\).  If \(	au_h\mu=\mu\), then \(h=0\).  Consequently, if linear maps \(T,T':\mathbb R^r	o\mathbb R^k\) and probability laws \(\mu,
u\) satisfy \(	au_{Tx}\mu=	au_{T'x}
u\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^r\), then \(\mu=
u\) and \(T=T'\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
The assertion is immediate for \(k=0\), so suppose \(k>0\).  Let
\[
 \phi_\mu(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^k}e^{\mathrm i t^{\mathsf T}z}\,d\mu(z).
\]
We first verify directly that \(\phi_\mu(t)\to1\) as \(t\to0\).  Given \(\eta>0\), continuity from below applied to the balls \(\{\lVert z\rVert\le R\}\) gives an \(R<\infty\) with \(\mu\{\lVert z\rVert>R\}<\eta\).  Since \(|e^{\mathrm i u}-1|\le |u|\),
\[
 |\phi_\mu(t)-1|
 \le \lVert t\rVert R+2\eta.
\]
Thus \(\phi_\mu\) is nonzero throughout some neighborhood of the origin.

If \(\tau_h\mu=\mu\), the characteristic functions obey
\[
 e^{\mathrm i t^{\mathsf T}h}\phi_\mu(t)=\phi_\mu(t).
\]
Were \(h\ne0\), one could choose \(t=ch\) with \(c>0\) so small that \(t\) lies in that neighborhood and \(0<c\lVert h\rVert^2<2\pi\).  The displayed equality would then give \(e^{\mathrm i c\lVert h\rVert^2}=1\), a contradiction.  Hence \(h=0\).

For the consequence, taking \(x=0\) gives \(\mu=\nu\).  Translating the asserted equality by \(-T'x\) shows that \(\mu\) is invariant under \((T-T')x\).  The first part gives \((T-T')x=0\) for every \(x\), so \(T=T'\).

added_lemmas.statement: If \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_r\) are mutually independent real random variables and every \(Z_i\) is nonconstant, where \(r\ge1\), then \(\sum_{i=1}^r Z_i\) is nonconstant.
added_lemmas.proof_tex: Suppose instead that \(\sum_i Z_i=c\) almost surely.  For each \(i\), the variable \(Z_i=c-\sum_{h\ne i}Z_h\) is measurable both with respect to \(\sigma(Z_i)\) and with respect to \(\sigma(Z_h:h\ne i)\).  These two sigma fields are independent.  Hence, for every Borel set \(A\), the event \(\{Z_i\in A\}\) is independent of itself and has probability zero or one.  Applying this to the half-lines with rational endpoints shows that the distribution function of \(Z_i\) takes only the values zero and one; monotonicity and right continuity then imply that it is the distribution function of a point mass.  Thus every \(Z_i\) is constant, contradicting the hypothesis.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(k,p\in\mathbb N_0\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times p}\).  There is a vector \(\xi^A\) of mutually independent nonconstant two-point, and hence non-Gaussian, sources such that the following holds for every \(q\in\mathbb N_0\), every \(D\in\mathbb R^{k\times q}\), and every vector \(\eta\) of mutually independent nonconstant real sources: if \(\mathcal L(A\xi^A)=\mathcal L(D\eta)\), then there are a surjection \(f:U_A\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero scalars \(a_i\), \(i\in U_A\), satisfying \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\).  Here \(U_A\) and \(U_D\) are the sets of nonzero columns; no location or moment condition is imposed on \(\eta\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(U=U_A\).  If \(U=\varnothing\), choose arbitrary independent two-point coordinates for \(\xi^A\).  Then \(A\xi^A=0\).  If \(U_D\ne\varnothing\), select \(j_0\in U_D\) and a linear functional \(b^{\mathsf T}\) with \(b^{\mathsf T}D_{:,j_0}\ne0\).  Among the independent scalar variables \((b^{\mathsf T}D_{:,j})\eta_j\), discard those with zero coefficient.  The remaining family is nonempty, mutually independent, and each member is nonconstant, while its sum would be the constant \(b^{\mathsf T}D\eta=0\).  This contradicts \(\text{lem:independent-sum-nondegenerate}\).  Thus \(U_D=\varnothing\), and the empty surjection proves the assertion.  When \(k=0\), both visible sets are empty by definition, so the same conclusion is immediate.

Suppose \(U\ne\varnothing\).  Let \(F\) be the subfield of \(\mathbb R\) generated by the finitely many entries of \(A\); it is countable.  Recursively choose positive numbers \((r_i)_{i\in U}\) algebraically independent over \(F\).  This is possible because at each finite stage the algebraic closure of the countable field already generated is countable, whereas every positive interval is uncountable.  Set
\[
 h_i=r_iA_{:,i},\qquad
 \Lambda=\bigoplus_{i\in U}\mathbb Z h_i.
\]
Indeed, if \(\sum_i m_ih_i=0\) with integers \(m_i\), each coordinate is a polynomial relation \(\sum_i m_iA_{vi}r_i=0\) over \(F\).  Algebraic independence makes every coefficient \(m_iA_{vi}\) zero, and the nonzero column \(A_{:,i}\) then gives \(m_i=0\).  Thus the displayed sum is direct.

Fix \(p_i\in(0,1)\), let the \(Z_i\) be independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities \(p_i\), and put \(\xi_i^A=r_iZ_i\) for \(i\in U\); use arbitrary independent nonconstant two-point laws on the zero columns.  All coordinates are nonconstant and non-Gaussian.  The output law has the \(2^{|U|}\) distinct support points
\[
 \left\{\sum_{i\in U}z_ih_i:z_i\in\{0,1\}\right\},                 \tag{1}
\]
and each point has positive mass.

Suppose this law is also that of \(\sum_{j\in U_D}Y_j\), where \(Y_j=D_{:,j}\eta_j\).  The topological support of a convolution contains the Minkowski sum of the supports of its factors: any neighborhoods of selected support points have positive probabilities, and independence gives positive probability to the sum of those neighborhoods.  Since (1) is finite, fixing one support point of every factor except \(Y_j\) injects \(\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), up to translation, into (1).  Hence every \(Y_j\) has finite support.  Each is nonconstant because \(D_{:,j}\ne0\) and \(\eta_j\) is nonconstant.

Choose \(y_j^0\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\).  For every \(y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)\), the two sums formed by using \(y\) and \(y_j^0\), while fixing support points of all other factors, both belong to (1).  Their difference lies in \(\Lambda\).  Freeness of \(\Lambda\) therefore gives a unique \(\nu_j(y)\in\mathbb Z^U\) such that
\[
 y-y_j^0=\sum_{i\in U}\nu_j(y)_ih_i.
\]
Define the Laurent probability polynomial
\[
 F_j(z)=\sum_{y\in\operatorname{supp}(Y_j)}Pr(Y_j=y)z^{\nu_j(y)}
 \in\mathbb R[z_i^{\pm1}:i\in U].
\]
The sum \(\sum_jy_j^0\) is itself a point of (1), so coefficientwise equality of the two convolution laws and injectivity of the exponent map into \(\Lambda\) give
\[
 \prod_{j\in U_D}F_j(z)
 =z^\gamma\prod_{i\in U}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\bigr)                 \tag{2}
\]
for some \(\gamma\in\mathbb Z^U\).

We record the algebra behind the next step.  A field is a unique-factorization domain.  If \(R\) is a unique-factorization domain, write every polynomial in \(R[z]\) as its coefficient content times a primitive polynomial.  Reducing a putative nonprimitive product modulo any prime divisor of all its coefficients shows that the product of two primitive polynomials is primitive.  Factorization over the fraction field, clearing denominators, and this primitive-product fact then give existence and uniqueness of factorization in \(R[z]\).  Induction over \(|U|\) proves that \(\mathbb R[z_i:i\in U]\) is a unique-factorization domain.  Localizing a factorization at the multiplicative set of monomials merely makes the variables into units and retains existence and uniqueness for all other irreducible factors.  Hence the Laurent ring \(\mathbb R[z_i^{\pm1}:i\in U]\) is a unique-factorization domain.

In this Laurent ring, each \((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\) is prime: quotienting by it substitutes the nonzero real value \(-(1-p_i)/p_i\) for \(z_i\) and leaves a Laurent polynomial domain in the other variables.  The factors for distinct \(i\)'s are nonassociated.  Unique factorization in (2) therefore supplies a partition \((I_j)_{j\in U_D}\) of \(U\) such that
\[
 F_j(z)=z^{\gamma_j}\prod_{i\in I_j}\bigl((1-p_i)+p_iz_i\bigr).    \tag{3}
\]
No \(I_j\) is empty, because an empty product in (3) would make \(Y_j\) constant.  If \(i\in I_j\), two support exponents in (3) differing only in coordinate \(i\) show that \(h_i\) is the difference of two support points of \(Y_j\).  Those points lie on \(\mathbb RD_{:,j}\), so \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,j}\) for some \(a_i\ne0\).  Defining \(f(i)=j\) when \(i\in I_j\) gives the required surjection and proportionalities.  The construction used only admissible two-point diagnostic sources and retained the original lattice \(\Lambda\) throughout.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(k,p,q\in\mathbb N_0\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{k\times p}\) and \(D\in\mathbb R^{k\times q}\), and let \(\mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(A)\) be the set of laws of \(A\xi\) as the coordinates of \(\xi\) range over arbitrary mutually independent nonconstant non-Gaussian real laws, with no location or moment restriction.  Then \(\mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(A)\subseteq\mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(D)\) if and only if there are a surjection \(f:U_A\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero real numbers \(a_i\), \(i\in U_A\), such that \(A_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\) for every \(i\in U_A\).  This includes \(k=0\), empty source families, and zero columns.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For necessity, apply the assumed containment to the two-point source vector \(\xi^A\) furnished by \(\text{lem:diagnostic-mixture-rigidity}\).  Its law must have a representation \(D\eta\) by independent nonconstant non-Gaussian sources, so that lemma gives exactly the asserted surjection and proportionalities.

Conversely, suppose \(f\) and \((a_i)\) exist, and fix any admissible source vector \(\xi\) for \(A\).  For \(j\in U_D\), define
\[
 \eta_j=\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\xi_i.                                    \tag{4}
\]
The nonempty fibers of the surjection are disjoint, so the variables in (4) are mutually independent.  Every summand is nonconstant and non-Gaussian.  The lemma \(\text{lem:independent-sum-nondegenerate}\) shows that \(\eta_j\) is nonconstant.  If \(\eta_j\) were Gaussian, the L\'evy--Cram\'er decomposition in \(\text{lem:levy-cramer-decomposition}\), applied inductively, would make every nonconstant summand \(a_i\xi_i\) Gaussian, contradicting admissibility.  Thus each \(\eta_j\) is non-Gaussian.  Give every zero column of \(D\) an arbitrary independent nonconstant non-Gaussian source, independent also of (4).  Columnwise proportionality yields
\[
 D\eta
 =\sum_{j\in U_D}D_{:,j}\sum_{i:f(i)=j}a_i\xi_i
 =\sum_{i\in U_A}A_{:,i}\xi_i
 =A\xi.
\]
This constructs a target representation for every source law without using expectations, variances, or location normalizations.  The empty cases reduce to the unique law at the origin and the empty surjection, as in the diagnostic lemma.

added_lemmas.statement: For fixed \(C\in\mathcal D_G\) and \(D\in\mathcal D_H\), every observable mixture law generated from \(C\) by arbitrary mutually independent nonconstant non-Gaussian real sources, with no location or moment restriction, is generated from \(D\) if and only if there exist a surjection \(f:U_C\twoheadrightarrow U_D\) and nonzero scalars \(a_i\) with \(C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}\) for every \(i\in U_C\).  Necessity is witnessed by admissible finite-support Bernoulli sources in their original jump lattice; sufficiency merges independent sources and preserves both nonconstancy and non-Gaussianity.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For a matrix \(A\), the observable laws obtained by varying the unrestricted admissible source coordinates are exactly \(\mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(A)\) in \(\text{lem:finite-mixture-containment-unrestricted}\).  Apply that lemma first with \(A=C\) and then with the candidate matrix \(D\).  It gives
\[
 \mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(C)\subseteq\mathscr L_{\mathrm{ng}}(D)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists f:U_C\twoheadrightarrow U_D\ \exists(a_i)_{i\in U_C}\in
 (\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})^{U_C}\ \forall i\in U_C:
 C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}.
\]
The diagnostic lemma proves the claimed original-lattice necessity, including proportional source columns and invisible columns.  The constructive direction of the finite-mixture theorem gives the merged target sources.  Its independent-sum and L\'evy--Cram\'er arguments establish nonconstancy and non-Gaussianity without a variance or centering premise.  This is precisely the claimed equivalence.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(\ell=0\), let \(A\subseteq X\), and suppose \(\mathcal I_A^{\mathrm{atom}}\subseteq\mathcal I\).  For every response-kernel tuple \(\mathbf K\) generated by a square exact-support mechanism with arbitrary independent nonconstant non-Gaussian sources, the observational law identifies the unordered projective row orbit \(\mathscr R(Q)\), the bipartite graph \(\mathbb G_b(\mathscr R(Q))\), and \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathscr R(Q))\).  For each \(i\in A\), the atomic kernel identifies \(T_i\) as the unique linear translation parameter satisfying \(K_{\{i\}}(x)=\tau_{T_ix}K_{\{i\}}(0)\); no expectation is required.  Lifting every residual-unmixing row \(v\) by \(\Lambda_i(v,T_i)=(v,-vT_i)\) recovers exactly the projective rows of \(Q\) except \([Q_{i,:}]\).  Hence \(\rho_i(\Pi_A\mathbf K)=[Q_{i,:}]\), normalization at coordinate \(i\) gives \(\operatorname{rec}_i(\Pi_A\mathbf K)=\operatorname{row}_i(B)\), and
\[
 \mathfrak M_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)
 =\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{row}}(\Pi_A\mathbf K)
 =\{\mu\in\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{obs}}(\mathscr R(Q)):
 \mu([Q_{i,:}])=i\text{ for every }i\in A\}.
\]
For \(A=\varnothing\) this is the observational perfect-matching representation; for \(A=X\), the full atomic family leaves only the true matching and recovers every row of \(B\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
When \(\ell=0\), \(C=Q^{-1}\) is square and invertible.  The observational law is the square mixture \(X=C\varepsilon\) of mutually independent nonconstant non-Gaussian sources.  By \(\text{lem:square-ica-uniqueness}\), its law determines the unordered projective columns of \(C\), equivalently
\[
 \mathscr R(Q)=\{[Q_{r,:}]:r\in X\}.
\]
Invertibility makes the row classes distinct.  Their zero patterns determine \(\mathbb G_b\), and its definition determines \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

Fix \(i\in A\) and put \(U=X\setminus\{i\}\).  The intervention-pushforward lemma gives
\[
 K_{\{i\}}(x)=\mathcal L(Q_{U,U}^{-1}\varepsilon_U+T_ix),
 \qquad T_i=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i}.                                    \tag{15}
\]
Taking \(x=0\) fixes the residual law.  The translation-rigidity lemma proves that \(T_i\) is the unique linear map translating that law to all the other kernels in (15), even when the sources have no moments.

At zero, (15) is a square invertible mixture of the \(n-1\) unaffected independent non-Gaussian sources.  Square ICA uniqueness identifies the projective rows of its unmixing matrix \(Q_{U,U}\).  If \(v=Q_{r,U}\) for \(r\in U\), then
\[
 vT_i=Q_{r,U}(-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i})=-Q_{r,i}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Lambda_i(v,T_i)_U=Q_{r,U},\qquad
 \Lambda_i(v,T_i)_i=-vT_i=Q_{r,i}.
\]
The lifted residual classes are exactly \(\{[Q_{r,:}]:r\ne i\}\), whose unique complement in the observational orbit is \([Q_{i,:}]\).  Looplessness gives \(Q_{ii}=1\), so normalization at coordinate \(i\) returns
\[
 e_i^{\mathsf T}-Q_{i,:}=\operatorname{row}_i(B).
\]

It remains to compare matchings.  Every observational matching normalizes a row-scaled permutation of \(Q\): for a permutation matrix \(P\) and nonsingular diagonal \(\Delta\),
\[
 Q^\mu=\Delta P Q,\qquad \varepsilon^\mu=\Delta P\varepsilon.       \tag{16}
\]
Scaling and permutation preserve independence, nonconstancy, and non-Gaussianity without any location or moment hypothesis, and (16) reproduces the observational law.  If \(\mu([Q_{i,:}])=i\), then \(P\) fixes row \(i\) and restricts to a permutation \(P_U\) of \(U\).  Hence
\[
 Q^\mu_{U,U}=\Delta_UP_UQ_{U,U},\quad
 Q^\mu_{U,i}=\Delta_UP_UQ_{U,i},\quad
 \varepsilon^\mu_U=\Delta_UP_U\varepsilon_U,
\]
which implies
\[
 -(Q^\mu_{U,U})^{-1}Q^\mu_{U,i}=-Q_{U,U}^{-1}Q_{U,i},\qquad
 (Q^\mu_{U,U})^{-1}\varepsilon^\mu_U=Q_{U,U}^{-1}\varepsilon_U.     \tag{17}
\]
Thus any observational matching satisfying all row constraints generates all required atomic kernels with the one global representation (16).  Conversely, a kernel-compatible matched mechanism must, by the recovery just proved from the common kernel tuple, assign the uniquely recovered class \([Q_{i,:}]\) to label \(i\) for every \(i\in A\).  This proves the displayed matching equality.  The conclusions for \(A=\varnothing\) and \(A=X\) follow immediately.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every loopless graph \(G\), the zero-allowed model and law sets decompose into their finitely many exact-support strata:
\[
 \mathfrak M^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)
 =\bigcup_{F\subseteq G}\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(F),
 \qquad
 \mathcal P^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)
 =\bigcup_{F\subseteq G}\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(F),                  \tag{19}
\]
where \(F\) ranges over all spanning loopless subgraphs of \(G\).  Each coefficient matrix belongs to the unique stratum with edge set \(\operatorname{supp}(B)\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex: Take a mechanism in \(\mathfrak M^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)\) and let \(F\) be the spanning loopless graph whose edge set is \(\operatorname{supp}(B)\).  By the zero-allowed support condition, \(F\subseteq G\).  The matrix has exact support \(F\), and every other clause---regime solvability, independence, nonconstancy, non-Gaussianity, and surgical intervention---is unchanged.  Hence the mechanism lies in \(\mathfrak M_{\mathcal I}(F)\).  Conversely, exact support \(F\subseteq G\) implies support contained in \(G\), so every exact-stratum mechanism lies in the zero-allowed class.  The stratum is unique because its edge set is the actual support of \(B\).  This proves the first equality in (19).  Applying the response-kernel map to both sides and using the definitions of the two law sets proves the second.  The union is finite because \(G\) has finitely many edges.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every finite \(X\), fixed \(\ell\), finite \(\mathcal I\ni\varnothing\), and loopless graph pair \(G,H\),
\[
 \mathcal P^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)\subseteq
 \mathcal P^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(H)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \operatorname{DownCover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H).                         \tag{20}
\]
Consequently, the two zero-allowed joint response-kernel sets are equal if and only if the two directed downward-closed cover conditions hold.  Equivalently, containment holds precisely when, for every exact subgraph \(F\subseteq G\) and every \(C\in\mathcal D_F\), one exact subgraph \(K\subseteq H\) and one tuple \((D,f,a)\) satisfy the source-partition equations and all response equalities simultaneously.  This is a finite-union theorem, not a monotone transfer of exact-support equivalence.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Assume first the law-set containment in (20).  Fix \(F\subseteq G\) and \(C\in\mathcal D_F\).  Exact mixing realization supplies a regime-solvable coefficient matrix with exact support \(F\) and observed mixing \(C\).  Choose the diagnostic source vector \(\xi^C\).  By the stratification lemma its kernel tuple belongs to \(\mathcal P^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)\), and hence to \(\mathcal P^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(H)\).  Apply the stratification lemma on \(H\) to the one target mechanism generating this tuple: its actual support is some \(K\subseteq H\), and exact mixing realization puts its observed mixing matrix \(D\) in \(\mathcal D_K\).  Equality of the observational diagnostic law and \(\text{lem:diagnostic-mixture-rigidity}\) give a surjection and scalars with
\[
 C_{:,i}=a_iD_{:,f(i)}.
\]
For each \(S\), equality of the full kernels, the intervention-pushforward identity, and probability-translation rigidity give \(T_S(C)=T_S(D)\).  Thus one \((K,D,f,a)\) satisfies all regimes, proving \(\operatorname{DownCover}_{\mathcal I}(G,H)\).

Conversely, take any mechanism in \(\mathfrak M^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(G)\).  Its actual support is a unique \(F\subseteq G\), and its observed mixing matrix \(C\) lies in \(\mathcal D_F\) by exact mixing realization.  A downward-cover witness supplies \(K\subseteq H\) and \((D,f,a)\).  Exact mixing realization constructs the target coefficient matrix on \(K\).  Group the original source coordinates over the fibers of \(f\), as in equation (10), and add arbitrary legal sources on zero columns.  The independent-sum and L\'evy--Cram\'er lemmas prove that the resulting common target sources are nonconstant and non-Gaussian.  The proportionality and simultaneous response equations imply the residual proportionalities (11), so intervention pushforward gives equality of every response kernel with the same target mechanism and source tuple.  This target exact-support \(K\)-mechanism belongs to \(\mathfrak M^{\le}_{\mathcal I}(H)\) because \(K\subseteq H\).  Directed containment follows.  Applying it in both directions proves equality.

The proof selected \(K\) only after fixing the exact stratum and \(C\), exactly as the finite condition permits.  It did not infer any inclusion or equality by monotonicity of exact-support law sets; (19) and the diagnostic construction establish the finite downward-closure union explicitly.

added_lemmas.statement:
Put \(e=N(N-1)\), \(q=|\mathcal I|\), \(p=nN\), and let \(\lambda\ge1\) bound the rational input bit length.  The downward-closed cover in either direction is decidable by the existing affine-chart compiler after finite disjunction over exact subgraphs.  With
\[
 s_{\le}=(q+N+1)2^{9N^2},\qquad d_{\le}=4N^3,
 \qquad \tau_{\le}=(\lambda+1)2^{9N^2},
\]
and
\[
 \mathsf B_{\le}
 = (\tau_{\le}+1)^2(s_{\le}+1)^{(p+1)(p+N+1)+1}
 (d_{\le}+1)^{c_{\mathrm{qe}}(p+1)(p+N+1)},                         \tag{21}
\]
one directed downward-closed decision takes at most \(2^e\mathsf B_{\le}\) bit operations, comparison takes at most \(2^{e+1}\mathsf B_{\le}\), and enumeration of the zero-allowed equivalence class modulo latent relabeling takes at most
\[
 2^e\bigl(2^{e+1}\mathsf B_{\le}+\ell!\,N^2\bigr)                  \tag{22}
\]
bit operations, apart from fixed linear encoding overhead.  The algorithm returns finite sign-cell certificates and contains no coefficient or source-law quantifier.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
For a fixed \(F\subseteq G\), replace the target-domain clause in (14) by the finite disjunction over \(K\subseteq H\):
\[
 \forall C\left[\operatorname{Dom}_F(C)\Longrightarrow
 \bigvee_{K\subseteq H}\ \bigvee_{U,W,f}
 \exists(D,a)\ \Theta_{K,f}(C,D,a)\right].                          \tag{23}
\]
Here \(\Theta_{K,f}\) is the explicit conjunction (12)--(13) with \(\operatorname{Dom}_K(D)\).  By the definition of downward cover and the zero-allowed coupled-equivalence theorem, all formulas (23), one for each \(F\subseteq G\), hold exactly when the directed zero-allowed containment holds.  Thus (23) is already free of structural coefficients and source distributions before elimination.

There are at most \(2^e<2^{N^2}\) choices of \(K\).  Multiplying the exact compiler's conservative number of atoms by this number gives at most
\[
 (q+N+1)2^{8N^2+N^2}=s_{\le}.
\]
The added operation is a Boolean disjunction, so the degree remains at most \(d_{\le}=4N^3\).  Encoding all copied atoms is bounded by the deliberately larger coefficient bit length \(\tau_{\le}\).  The quantified real-variable blocks remain \(C\) of size \(p\), and \((D,a)\) of size at most \(p+N\), because \(K,U,W,f\) are finite discrete choices rather than real variables.  The cited effective elimination lemma therefore gives the bound \(\mathsf B_{\le}\) in (21) for each fixed \(F\).

At most \(2^e\) subgraphs \(F\) are checked, proving the directed bound.  Two directions prove the comparison bound.  Finally test the \(2^e\) labeled candidate graphs and canonicalize each under at most \(\ell!\) latent permutations, at \(N^2\) bit comparisons apiece, to obtain (22).  Every loop is finite, and the sign-cell output retains zero signs and all lower-dimensional strata, so the algorithm terminates with a checkable exact certificate.

prose_updates.tldr: The paper characterizes equality of joint perfect-intervention response-kernel sets for finite latent linear non-Gaussian feedback graphs. At the exact-support level, an affine and Hall--Rado realization theorem, an unrestricted visible-source partition theorem, and simultaneous response constraints give a sound-and-complete coupled invariant and an effective sign-cell compiler. A new downward-closure theorem then proves explicitly that the zero-allowed class is the finite union of exact-support strata and gives its own finite coupled criterion; no monotone transfer of exact-support equality is assumed. Response slopes are identified as unique probability-law translations, so population identification requires neither centering nor moments. proofs.proof_tex:
We first prove equality of the observational model sets without using centering or moments.  By Definition \texttt{def:witness-mechanisms}, an arbitrary mechanism on \(G_\star\) has equations
\[
 L=\varepsilon_L,\qquad
 X_1=cL+aX_2+\varepsilon_1,\qquad
 X_2=bX_1+\varepsilon_2,\qquad
 X_3=dL+\varepsilon_3,
 \tag{1}
\]
where Assumption \texttt{ass:exact-support} and the displayed admissibility condition give
\[
 a\ne0,\qquad b\ne0,\qquad c\ne0,\qquad d\ne0,
 \qquad 1-ab\ne0.
 \tag{2}
\]
Define the \(H_\star\) coefficients
\[
 \alpha=b^{-1},\qquad \beta=a^{-1},\qquad
 \gamma=-ca^{-1},\qquad \delta=d
 \tag{3}
\]
and define its sources on the same probability space by
\[
 \eta_L=\varepsilon_L,\qquad
 \eta_1=-b^{-1}\varepsilon_2,\qquad
 \eta_2=-a^{-1}\varepsilon_1,\qquad
 \eta_3=\varepsilon_3.
 \tag{4}
\]
Every division in (3)--(4) is licensed by (2).  Equation (4) is a permutation followed by nonzero coordinatewise rescaling.  Hence Assumption \texttt{ass:source-independence} is preserved.  It also preserves Assumption \texttt{ass:source-nondegeneracy}: if \(rY\) were almost surely constant for \(r\ne0\), then \(Y=r^{-1}(rY)\) would be almost surely constant.  It preserves Assumption \texttt{ass:source-nongaussianity} for the same reason: if \(rY\) were Gaussian, then \(Y=r^{-1}(rY)\) would be Gaussian.  If centering or Assumption \texttt{ass:source-second-moment} is imposed on the subfamily under consideration, it too is preserved, since
\[
 \mathbb E[rY]=r\mathbb E[Y],
 \qquad
 \mathbb E[(rY)^2]=r^2\mathbb E[Y^2].
 \tag{5}
\]

The endogenous vector solving (1) satisfies the transformed equations sample by sample.  Indeed, using the equations for \(X_2\) and \(X_1\), respectively,
\[
 \alpha X_2+\eta_1
 =b^{-1}(X_2-\varepsilon_2)=X_1,
 \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
 \gamma L+\beta X_1+\eta_2
 =-ca^{-1}L+a^{-1}(X_1-\varepsilon_1)=X_2.
 \tag{7}
\]
Also \(L=\eta_L\) and \(X_3=\delta L+\eta_3\).  Thus (6)--(7) are precisely the \(H_\star\) equations and the two observed vectors agree almost surely.

The transformation stays in the exact-support class.  All four coefficients in (3) are nonzero by (2), and
\[
 1-\alpha\beta
 =1-\frac1{ab}
 =\frac{ab-1}{ab}\ne0.
 \tag{8}
\]
For completeness, regime solvability does not conceal a stability condition.  Because \(S\subseteq\{X_1,X_2,X_3\}\) and the only directed cycle is the \(X_1,X_2\) two-cycle, direct expansion of the relevant principal structural matrix gives
\[
 \det Q^{G_\star}_{V\setminus S,V\setminus S}
 =\begin{cases}
 1-ab,&S\cap\{X_1,X_2\}=\varnothing,\\
 1,&S\cap\{X_1,X_2\}\ne\varnothing,
 \end{cases}
 \tag{9}
\]
and the analogous determinant for \(H_\star\) is obtained by replacing \(ab\) by \(\alpha\beta\).  Equations (2), (8), and (9) verify Assumption \texttt{ass:regime-solvability} for every observed intervention target.

Conversely, let an arbitrary \(H_\star\) mechanism have nonzero coefficients \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) and \(1-\alpha\beta\ne0\).  Set
\[
 a=\beta^{-1},\qquad b=\alpha^{-1},\qquad
 c=-\gamma\beta^{-1},\qquad d=\delta,
 \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
 \varepsilon_L=\eta_L,\qquad
 \varepsilon_1=-\beta^{-1}\eta_2,\qquad
 \varepsilon_2=-\alpha^{-1}\eta_1,\qquad
 \varepsilon_3=\eta_3.
 \tag{11}
\]
The quantities in (10) are nonzero and
\[
 1-ab=1-\frac1{\alpha\beta}
 =\frac{\alpha\beta-1}{\alpha\beta}\ne0.
 \tag{12}
\]
The preservation argument following (4) applies to (11), and substitution shows that (10)--(11) invert (3)--(4).  We have therefore constructed a bijection of the entire admissible observational parameter spaces, not merely of generic subsets or their closures.  Equations (6)--(7) show equality of the coupled observed solutions.  Definitions \texttt{def:response-kernel-tuple} and \texttt{def:graph-law-set} now yield
\[
 \mathcal P_{\{\varnothing\}}(G_\star)
 =\mathcal P_{\{\varnothing\}}(H_\star).
 \tag{13}
\]

We next record the finite-moment covariance calculation.  Assumption \texttt{ass:perfect-intervention} says that \(\operatorname{do}(X_1=z)\) replaces only the equation for \(X_1\).  For (1), the unaffected equations give
\[
 X_2=bz+\varepsilon_2,\qquad
 X_3=d\varepsilon_L+\varepsilon_3.
 \tag{14}
\]
The first variable in (14) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(\varepsilon_2)\), and the second is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(\varepsilon_L,\varepsilon_3)\).  Assumption \texttt{ass:source-independence} therefore makes \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) independent, without any moment condition.  If Assumption \texttt{ass:source-second-moment} is imposed for this covariance clause, bilinearity of covariance and independence give
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_{G_\star}(X_2,X_3)
 =d\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_L)
  +\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3)=0.
 \tag{15}
\]

For an arbitrary \(H_\star\) mechanism, surgical intervention gives
\[
 X_2=\gamma\eta_L+\beta z+\eta_2,\qquad
 X_3=\delta\eta_L+\eta_3.
 \tag{16}
\]
When the sources in (16) have finite second moments, source independence gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Cov}_{H_\star}(X_2,X_3)
 &=\gamma\delta\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L)
   +\gamma\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_L,\eta_3)
   +\delta\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_2,\eta_L)
   +\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_2,\eta_3)\\
 &=\gamma\delta\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{17}
\]
Assumption \texttt{ass:exact-support} gives \(\gamma\delta\ne0\).  Assumption \texttt{ass:source-nondegeneracy} and square integrability give \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta_L)>0\), so (17) is nonzero.  For the paired mechanism (3)--(4), \(\gamma=-c/a\), \(\delta=d\), and \(\eta_L=\varepsilon_L\).  By the definition of \(\sigma_L^2\), equation (17) becomes
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_{H_\star}(X_2,X_3)
 =-\frac ca d\sigma_L^2\ne0.
 \tag{18}
\]

It remains to prove separation of the full model sets when their general source laws need not possess moments.  Take the legal coefficients
\[
 a=\frac12,\qquad b=\frac13,\qquad c=d=1,
 \tag{19}
\]
and let the four \(G_\star\) sources be mutually independent symmetric random signs.  Each source is centered, bounded, nonconstant, non-Gaussian, and has finite second moment.  Equations (9) and (19) show that this mechanism is solvable in every regime.  Let \(\mathbf K^G\) denote its joint response-kernel tuple.  At \(z=0\), (14) shows that the \(X_2\) and \(X_3\) coordinates of its singleton-intervention kernel are square integrable and have covariance zero.

Suppose for contradiction that \(\mathbf K^G\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H_\star)\).  By Definition \texttt{def:graph-law-set}, one \(H_\star\) mechanism with one common source tuple must then reproduce every component of \(\mathbf K^G\).  In particular, its kernel at \(\operatorname{do}(X_1=0)\) has the same joint law.  Hence each variable on the right side of (16), with \(z=0\), is square integrable.  Apply Lemma \texttt{lem:square-integrable-independent-summands} first to the independent summands \(\delta\eta_L\) and \(\eta_3\), and then to the independent summands \(\gamma\eta_L\) and \(\eta_2\).  It follows that
\[
 \mathbb E[\eta_L^2]<\infty,\qquad
 \mathbb E[\eta_2^2]<\infty,\qquad
 \mathbb E[\eta_3^2]<\infty,
 \tag{20}
\]
where division by \(\gamma^2\) or \(\delta^2\) is valid because Assumption \texttt{ass:exact-support} gives \(\gamma\delta\ne0\).  Thus the covariance calculation (17) is licensed even though no moment condition was imposed on the ambient population class.  Assumption \texttt{ass:source-nondegeneracy} makes the resulting variance strictly positive, so (17) gives a nonzero covariance, contradicting equality with the covariance-zero \(G_\star\) kernel.  Therefore
\[
 \mathbf K^G\notin\mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H_\star),
 \qquad
 \mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(G_\star)\ne
 \mathcal P_{\mathcal I}(H_\star)
 \quad\text{whenever }\{X_1\}\in\mathcal I.
 \tag{21}
\]

The causal objects in (13) and (21) are sets of population perfect-intervention response kernels, not observational regressions.  No treatment-overlap or positivity condition is needed because intervention values are externally fixed.  All matrices are finite dimensional, every inversion was justified by (2), (8), (9), or (12), and no boundary or limiting argument is used.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(U\) and \(W\) be independent real-valued random variables.  If \(\mathbb E[(U+W)^2]<\infty\), then \(\mathbb E[U^2]<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E[W^2]<\infty\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Because \(W\) is real valued, the events \(\{|W|\le r\}\), \(r\in\mathbb N\), increase to the whole sample space.  Hence there is an \(R\in\mathbb N\) for which
\[
 p_R:=\Pr(|W|\le R)>0.
\]
On the event \(\{|U|>2R,\ |W|\le R\}\), the triangle inequality gives
\[
 |U+W|\ge |U|-|W|\ge |U|/2.
\]
All integrands below are nonnegative, so the inequalities remain valid even before integrability has been established.  Independence of \(U\) and \(W\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E[(U+W)^2]
 &\ge \mathbb E\!\left[(U+W)^2
       \mathbf 1_{\{|U|>2R\}}\mathbf 1_{\{|W|\le R\}}\right]\\
 &\ge \frac14\mathbb E\!\left[U^2
       \mathbf 1_{\{|U|>2R\}}\mathbf 1_{\{|W|\le R\}}\right]\\
 &=\frac{p_R}{4}\mathbb E\!\left[U^2
       \mathbf 1_{\{|U|>2R\}}\right].
 \end{aligned}
\]
The left side is finite and \(p_R>0\), so the last expectation is finite.  The complementary part is bounded by
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[U^2\mathbf 1_{\{|U|\le2R\}}\right]\le4R^2.
\]
Thus \(\mathbb E[U^2]<\infty\).  Interchanging \(U\) and \(W\) proves \(\mathbb E[W^2]<\infty\).
